drills.title: Contracts from a stop
drills.question: Capital $5m, risk 1% per trade. Long an index future at 2,000 with a stop at 1,960; multiplier $50. How many contracts, and what is the loss if the market gaps to 1,920?
drills.solution: Risk = $50,000. Loss per contract at the stop = 40 x 50 = $2,000. n = 25. A gap to 1,920 loses 80 x 50 x 25 = $100,000, twice the plan.
common_mistakes: Dividing by the price instead of the stop distance
Treating the stop as a guaranteed exit
drills.intuition: The stop rule sizes the loss you plan for; the gap sets the loss you get.
drills.takeaway: Size off the plausible gap, not the stop.

drills.title: Half-Kelly in one line
drills.question: Excess return 8%, volatility 20%, r = 0. Give the Kelly leverage, the maximum excess growth, and the excess growth at half-Kelly.
common_mistakes: Assuming half the bet gives half the growth
Forgetting that growth falls to zero at 2x Kelly
drills.intuition: Growth is a parabola in size; its top is flat.
drills.takeaway: Half-Kelly keeps 75% of growth for 25% of the variance.

drills.title: Two loans, zero VaR
drills.question: Two independent $2m loans each default with probability 3% (total loss). Give the 95% VaR of one loan, the 95% VaR of the pair, and the 95% ES of the pair. What does this say about VaR limits?

rubric: Shows P(any default) = 5.91% > 5%, so pair VaR is one loan
States that VaR is not subadditive here while ES is
Concludes that credit books need ES or default-scenario limits

drills.solution: One loan: 3% < 5%, VaR = 0. Pair: P(no default) = 0.9409, so P(loss) = 5.91% and VaR = $2m. ES: (0.0009 x 4m + 0.0491 x 2m)/0.05 = $2.036m, below the $4.8m sum of standalone ES (1.2m each).
common_mistakes: Adding standalone VaRs (0) to get the pair
drills.intuition: A quantile ignores everything beyond it.
drills.takeaway: VaR limits reward books of small-probability, large-loss positions.

drills.title: Margin call and covenant on the same morning
drills.question: Long 20 index futures ($50 multiplier) with $600,000 in the account; initial/maintenance margin $24,000/$22,000. Separately, a property worth $22m carries a $15m loan with a 75% LTV covenant. Give the fall in points that triggers the margin call, the call after a 300-point fall, and the cure if the property value falls 12%.

rubric: Uses maintenance margin for the trigger and initial margin for the call
Computes cure = loan - 0.75 x new value
Adds the two cash demands and compares with available liquidity
States which position to cut if cash is insufficient

drills.solution: Maintenance total = 20 x 22,000 = $440,000. Trigger = (600,000 - 440,000)/(20 x 50) = 160 points. After 300 points: loss = 300 x 50 x 20 = $300,000, equity $300,000; the call restores initial margin 20 x 24,000 = $480,000, so the call is $180,000. Property: new value 22.0 x 0.88 = $19.36m; cure = 15.0 - 0.75 x 19.36 = $0.48m. Total cash needed the same week: $660,000.
common_mistakes: Applying the covenant to the original value
drills.intuition: Financing turns price moves into dated cash demands.
drills.takeaway: Size positions so that the joint cash demand in a stress fits inside free cash.

drills.title: Stop or put before a weekend
drills.question: Long 10 index futures at 4,000 ($50 multiplier), stop at 3,880. A weekend event is scheduled. Monday could open at 3,700. A 3,880 put costs 30 points. Give the planned loss, the loss if the market gaps to 3,700, and the maximum loss with the puts. Should you buy the puts?

rubric: Computes planned and gap losses from the stop and the open
Adds the premium to the stop-distance loss for the hedged maximum
Compares the premium with the probability-weighted extra gap loss
Considers the alternative of cutting size over the event instead of buying insurance

drills.solution: Planned = 120 x 50 x 10 = $60,000. Gap = 300 x 50 x 10 = $150,000. With puts: 60,000 + 30 x 50 x 10 = $75,000 whatever the open. The puts cost $15,000; they pay off relative to the stop if P(gap) x extra loss exceeds that, e.g. a 1-in-6 chance of the $90,000 extra loss. Halving size over the event is the cheaper alternative if the view is not event-specific.
common_mistakes: Assuming the stop fills at 3,880 on a gap open
Treating the premium as wasted if no gap occurs
drills.intuition: A stop is an order; a put is a contract.
drills.takeaway: Buy hard limits for dated events; size down when you cannot price the event.

drills.title: Liquidity-adjusted VaR for a REIT block
drills.question: You hold 800,000 shares at $25. ADV 200,000; max participation 20%; daily vol 1.8%; stressed spread 1.2%. Give days to liquidate, one-day 99% VaR, liquidation-horizon VaR under even daily sales, and LVaR.
common_mistakes: Scaling by sqrt(20) as if the whole block were held 20 days
Ignoring the spread, or using the normal-day spread
drills.intuition: A block you cannot sell today carries more than one day of risk, but less than T days of full exposure.
drills.takeaway: Charge illiquid positions for their exit horizon, or cut them to what you can sell before your stop.

drills.title: A low-VaR fund with private loans
drills.question: A manager seeks a $10m allocation. Reported one-day 99% VaR is 1.2% of NAV, from two years of daily data. 30% of NAV is in hotel bridge loans marked quarterly by the manager. Reported maximum drawdown is 3%. Fund-level leverage and redemption terms are 'available after commitment'. Do you allocate?

rubric: Recognizes that quarterly self-marks on 30% of NAV suppress measured VaR and drawdown (smoothing)
Notes that two years of data may contain no stress episode and that VaR omits the private book
Identifies undisclosed leverage and redemption terms as decisive missing information (financing and liquidity risk)
Requests a stress test of the loan book, the facility terms, and third-party marks
Concludes that the best action is to abstain until the information is provided, and states what would change that

drills.solution: Abstain. The reported risk numbers measure the liquid 70% and a smoothed 30%. Without fund leverage, facility covenants and redemption gates you cannot compute the cash path in stress, which is where ruin occurs. Ask for the facility agreement, a scenario P&L for a 25-35% hotel value decline, third-party marks and the redemption terms. Re-evaluate if they are provided and the stress loss with leverage fits your limit.
common_mistakes: Accepting a low VaR as low risk
Treating a small reported drawdown on self-marked assets as evidence of skill
drills.intuition: A risk number that excludes the risky part is a measure of what was measured.

drills.title: Investment committee: stress and re-limit
drills.question: NAV $30m: $10m Treasuries (D 7, C 60), long 10 ES at 5,000, $5m equity in a $16m hotel with an $11m non-recourse loan. Scenario: yields +100 bp, ES -25%, hotel -20%. Compute P&L by leg, the total and % of NAV, then recommend changes to the book.

rubric: Computes the Treasury leg with duration and convexity
Applies the futures multiplier to notional
Caps the hotel equity loss at the equity and recomputes from value minus loan
Identifies the hotel as 71% of the loss and the rate-equity correlation as positive in this scenario
Recommends a change (lower hotel LTV, cure reserve, or reduced duration) with its effect on the stress loss
States a second scenario in which the Treasury leg behaves differently

drills.solution: Treasuries: 10m x (-7 x 0.01 + 0.5 x 60 x 0.0001) = -$670,000. ES: 10 x 5,000 x 50 x -0.25 = -$625,000. Hotel: 16m x 0.8 = 12.8m; equity 1.8m; loss -$3.2m. Total -$4,495,000 = -14.98% of NAV. The hotel is 71% of the loss. In an inflationary shock both hedges and risk assets lose; in a deflationary crash the Treasuries would offset. Cutting the hotel loan to $9m (with $2m more equity) lowers the stress loss rate on hotel equity and removes covenant risk, at a cost in levered return.
common_mistakes: Treating Treasuries as a hedge in every scenario
Reporting the loss as a percentage of gross assets rather than NAV
drills.intuition: A stress test ranks which assumption hurts most if wrong.
drills.takeaway: Re-limit on stress loss and cash demand, not on VaR.
